kicker: You don't need to write code yourself — AI is the carpenter; your job is to draw a really clear plan and check every cut.
summary: The best AI game makers aren't the fastest typists — they describe clearly and fix in small steps.

game.name: Koi & Moon Pond
game.pitch: A koi swims under the night pond; drag or tap to make it catch falling moon pieces and dodge dry leaves.

quiz.q: Your game has a bug: the koi stays still instead of following your finger. Which report helps AI fix it best?
options: Send AI a screenshot of the game and add: “the fish won't swim, fix it”
Paste the whole long code file and ask AI to find the bug
Ask AI to rewrite the whole game from scratch
Paste the red error (F12) + “expected it to follow, but it stays”
quiz.explain: The red error line (in the Console, opened with F12) plus “expected – saw” points at exactly what broke, so AI fixes the root instead of guessing.

blueprint.label: A plan before carving
blueprint.art: Ink painting: a dark drawing room, a six-sided paper andon lamp glowing on the table. Each face is one piece of the design; under the front face hang two paper strips, the two ways it could go. Choose a strip: it sticks to the face, the lamp throws that part of the game sharp onto the wall — the pond, the fish, a piece of moon — and a line is written into spec.md on the table. With all six faces done, the whole game stands on the wall before a single line of code.
blueprint.lampAria: The spec lantern, face {n}: {piece}. Left and right arrow keys turn it.
blueprint.prompt: Pick one paper strip for each face of the lamp
blueprint.group: The six pieces of the plan

pieces.label: One-line idea
options: A fun game about a fish
A koi snaps falling moon shards, dodging dry leaves

pieces.label: Rules in 3 lines
options: Moon +1 · dry leaf costs 1 heart · the moon falls faster and faster

pieces.label: Controls
options: Drag or tap, the fish swims after your finger

pieces.label: Win / lose
options: After 30 seconds or 3 lost hearts, show the score

pieces.label: Style
options: Ink painting: indigo night, ivory moon, few colours

facts.text: GitHub (Spec Kit) advises: write down clearly what you want first, then let that description guide the AI writing the code.

insight.text: A vague strip leaves a blurred shadow: AI has to guess. A clear strip makes it sharp — that is the game AI will build.

blueprint.detail: The last two lines keep AI from overdoing it and tell you when to stop.
blueprint.specDecode: spec.md = the sheet that describes the game; AI reads it before writing code
extra: 30 seconds of play with no errors on a phone

pens.label: Choosing a pen
pens.art: Ink painting: a night workshop. On an easel, a wooden frame holds a stone basin with a koi, seen from above; under the lamp, a bamboo pot of five pens. The three flat pens can only paint a sheet of paper — drag it and the sheet just slides; the Three.js pen turns the frame into a 3D window — drag and the whole pond turns in the moonlight; the Godot/Unity pen pulls the camera back over the whole garden and the frame becomes a screen's bezel.
pens.frameAria: The koi pond picture on the easel
pens.frameHint: Flat pens: drag or use the arrow keys to slide the sheet. 3D pens: drag or use the arrow keys to turn the pond, + and − to move closer.
pens.prompt: Tap each brush in the pot

pens.name: Phaser
pens.fits: 2D games with many levels, animated characters, collisions

facts.text: Phaser has moved to version 4; the latest when checked was 4.2.1, released 9 July 2026.

insight.text: A quick rule: small 2D game → Canvas or Phaser; 3D in the browser → Three.js; a big game needing an app → Godot or Unity.

pens.detail: There is no “best” pen. Name the pen in your instruction so AI doesn't pick something you don't know. Library versions change often — check the official site.
pens.dragPrompt: Drag inside the frame to try this brush
pens.otherFlat: Now pick a flat brush: Canvas, p5.js or Phaser
pens.other3d: Now pick the Three.js or Godot / Unity brush
pens.askNote: Copy this line to AI as it is; the odd words are tool names, AI knows them.

carve.label: Carve one cut at a time, save each step
carve.art: Ink painting: the wood shop at night, seen at table height. A cypress block on its carving stand stands against the open door onto the moonlit lake, the moon behind it rimming its outline in light. Seven stones in a row along the bench's front edge are the seven steps; each one placed right is a stroke of the mallet — chips fly and the block becomes one stage more of a fish: chalk lines, rough cut, split tail, fins, scales, eye. The work lamp can be dragged so its warm light rakes the wood; the code lies rolled up on the bench.
carve.lampAria: Work lamp: drag left or right, or use the arrow keys, to light the wood
carve.prompt: Tap the stones in the order you'd do them
carve.pathAria: A seven-stone path for making a web game
carve.keys: Tap in turn, or use number keys 1 to 7.
carve.done: The path is lit. Open your take-away card.

steps.label: Create the project
steps.detail: Once: have AI walk you through creating the project with Vite (a tool that sets up a web page skeleton).
steps.why: A ready skeleton and test server, no manual setup.

steps.label: Have AI build the frame
steps.detail: Paste the game description (spec.md) and say: build a frame that runs, it needn't look good yet.
steps.why: Get something running first; every feature hangs on it.

steps.label: Run it on your computer
steps.detail: One command (npm run dev) opens the game in the browser; save and you see it at once.
steps.why: Seeing the result after each change catches mistakes early.

steps.label: Add one feature
steps.detail: Ask for exactly one thing, test it, then ask for the next.
steps.why: One thing at a time, so you know what broke what.

steps.label: Fix bugs with evidence
steps.detail: Paste the red error line (Console, opened with F12) + “expected… but saw…”.
steps.why: Evidence lets AI fix the root cause, not guess.

steps.label: Save a checkpoint, next feature
steps.detail: Checkpoint = a saved version of the game (git commit); if something breaks you can go back. Then return to step 4 with the next feature.
steps.why: One checkpoint per feature: if it breaks, go back instead of starting over.

steps.label: Put it online
steps.detail: Once, at the end: have AI package it (npm run build) and publish to GitHub Pages, Vercel or Netlify.
steps.why: With a link, friends can play right away.

prompts: Create a Vite project with the vanilla template named koi-pond and explain each generated file.
Here is my spec.md. Build a running skeleton with Canvas 2D: the pond surface and one koi. No score or sound yet.
Show me how to run the game on my computer, and what I should see on screen.
Add exactly one feature: dry leaves fall slowly, and touching one costs the koi 1 heart. Keep everything else the same.
Expected the koi to follow the mouse, but it stays still. Console error: [PASTE]. Find the root cause and fix it with as little change as possible.
Save a checkpoint of what we just changed, with a short line describing it. If the next step breaks, show me how to go back to it.
Walk me step by step through building and publishing the game on GitHub Pages, including the usual pitfalls.
carve.codeAria: Sample code: a koi following your finger on Canvas 2D

notes.text: Grab the canvas (drawing frame) already on the page.
Grab the 2D “brush” to draw on it.
The koi: where it is (x, y) and where it wants to go (tx, ty).
Wherever the finger or mouse goes, the koi wants to swim there.
Each frame the koi swims 8% of the remaining distance — so it glides, never jerks.
Repaint the night pond, erasing the previous frame.
Draw the body: a vermilion ellipse.
Ask the browser to call again next frame — this is the game loop.

facts.text: Vite creates a project with npm create vite@latest and runs at localhost:5173; it needs Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+.
npm run build creates a dist folder; Vite's docs explain publishing to GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel and more.

insight.text: One cut per feature, and save a checkpoint after each cut. If something breaks, go back to the last checkpoint instead of carving again from scratch.

carve.detail: You don't need to remember git commands: tell AI “save a checkpoint of this change” or “go back to the last checkpoint”. Commands and versions change — follow Vite's official guide.

layers.label: The game grows layer by layer
layers.art: Ink painting: an empty round stone basin floating in the dark over its soft shadow. Above it hang seven sheets of tracing paper, apart, each one layer of the game — water, koi, the leading hand, falling moon, score and hearts, the sound of water, fireflies — its name on the front edge. Touch the lit sheet: it sinks into the basin with a ring of ripples, the prompt for that layer is written beside the basin and the pond comes one step more alive. With all seven, the view rises over the basin and the real game plays in its water.
layers.prompt: Tap the glowing sheet to drop it into the basin
layers.promptLabel: The prompt that made this layer

layers.name: Water
layers.prompt: Paint an indigo night pond with gentle ripples.

layers.name: Koi
layers.prompt: Add one red-and-white koi whose body bends as it swims.

layers.name: Controls
layers.prompt: Make the fish swim after a finger or the mouse.

layers.name: Falling moon
layers.prompt: Drop moon shards; when the fish touches one, +1 point.

layers.name: Dry leaves
layers.prompt: Add slowly falling dry leaves; touching one costs 1 of 3 hearts.

layers.name: End of round
layers.prompt: After 30 seconds or no hearts left, show the score in an ensō circle.

layers.name: Sound
layers.prompt: A soft “plop” when it snaps the moon; off by default.

play.region: Koi & Moon Pond: drag, tap or use the arrow keys to swim; catch moon pieces, dodge dry leaves.
play.how: Drag or tap to guide the koi · catch the moon · dodge dry leaves
play.endAria: Game over. You caught {n} moon pieces.
play.still: Reduced motion: the moon falls slowly, no ripples.

facts.text: The instructions here are examples of breaking a game into small steps.

insight.text: Seven short instructions, one feature each, test after each one — the game grows without breaking.

layers.detail: After a round, open the take-away card: the full prompt pack to rebuild this game from scratch.
layers.wrongOrder: Not this layer yet — drop the “{name}” sheet first

vibe.label: Is coding by feel enough?
vibe.art: Ink painting: looking down into a deep, clear pond. On the surface the koi game is playing: the fish on its round, a shard of moon, the moon's broken road. On the bed, the game's source code is written in ink on flat stones, caustics drifting over it. Along the near edge stand five big candle stones, out of focus. Touch one: its candle lights, who spoke is written on the water and the pond changes with them: the focus at the surface or down on the code, red cracks through half the lines, a paper lantern with a red seal floating up, a bamboo fence growing round the shallows. Drag up or down on the water to move the focus yourself. With all five, the water stills and an ensō appears.
vibe.prompt: Tap each candle to hear five people

view.text: Andrej Karpathy (Feb 2025): let AI write it, “forget that the code even exists” — fine for throwaway weekend projects.
Simon Willison: if you've read, tested and can explain the code, that's normal programming, not vibe coding anymore.
Veracode (a security company, its own report): tested 80 coding tasks on 100+ AI models; about 45% of the solutions had security holes.
Collins Dictionary named “vibe coding” its 2025 Word of the Year — the practice has gone mainstream.
One beginner, for example: “A small game is a safe place to practise — if it breaks, start again, nobody loses money.”

common.text: For a small game, let AI write it and play-test. With logins, money or users' data, someone must read the code carefully.

vibe.detail: The koi game runs in the browser with no accounts or payments, so the risk is low. When an app has logins, money or user data, ask someone who knows code to review it.
vibe.question: Vibe coding: ask AI to write the code, run it, never read the code.
vibe.focusPrompt: Drag up and down on the pond to look down at the code on the bottom
